los.text: Explain the main causes, pathophysiology and signs and symptoms of patients presenting with heart disease and angina / MI (include referred pain mechanism)
los.html:
Causes of myocardial ischaemia
  • Coronary atherosclerosis (vast majority)
  • Others: coronary spasm (Prinzmetal, cocaine)
  • Embolism
  • Dissection (SCAD: young women, peripartum)
  • Vasculitis (Kawasaki)
  • Aortic stenosis/HOCM
  • Anaemia
  • Tachyarrhythmia
  • Thyrotoxicosis (demand ischaemia = type 2 MI).
Risk factorsAge, male, FHx premature CHD, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity, inactivity, CKD, South Asian ethnicity, deprivation, RA/SLE.
Angina
  • Ischaemia when O₂ demand > supply (exercise, cold, emotion, meals) → central tight/heavy chest pain, radiating to left arm, jaw, neck
  • Relieved by rest/GTN within ~5 min.
  • Associated breathlessness.
  • NICE: typical = all 3 of (constricting discomfort, precipitated by exertion, relieved by rest/GTN).
MI
  • Prolonged ischaemia (>20–30 min) → necrosis.
  • Pain at rest >15 min, not relieved by GTN, with sweating, nausea, vomiting, breathlessness, anxiety ("sense of doom")
  • May be "silent" (diabetes, elderly, women: atypical: breathlessness, fatigue, epigastric pain).
  • Signs: pale, clammy, tachy/bradycardia, hypotension, S4, signs of HF.
Referred pain mechanism
  • Cardiac visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibres to T1–T5 dorsal horns, where they converge on the same second-order neurons as somatic afferents from the chest wall and medial arm (T1–T2 dermatomes).
  • The brain misattributes visceral pain to the somatic area (convergence–projection theory).
  • Jaw/neck via cervical sympathetic ganglia
  • Inferior MI can cause epigastric pain.

los.text: Describe the causes of atherosclerosis and explain how atherosclerotic plaques form and their consequences
los.html:
• Response-to-injury hypothesis:
1. Endothelial dysfunction/injury(hypertension shear stress, smoking, hyperglycaemia, LDL, turbulent flow at branch points)↑ permeability, adhesion molecules (VCAM-1), ↓ NO.
2LDL enters intima → oxidised.
3Monocytes adhere and migrate → macrophages take up oxLDL via scavenger receptors → foam cells → fatty streak (from childhood).
4
  • Cytokines/growth factors (PDGF)
  • → smooth muscle cell migration from media to intima and proliferation
  • → collagen
  • → fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core (cholesterol crystals, debris) = fibrofatty atheroma.
  • Calcification.
  • T cells, chronic inflammation.
Stable plaqueThick fibrous cap, small lipid core → fixed stenosis → stable angina, claudication.
Vulnerable plaque
  • Thin cap, large lipid core, many macrophages (MMPs digest cap)
  • → rupture/erosion
  • → exposes thrombogenic core (tissue factor)
  • → platelet aggregation + thrombosis
  • → ACS, stroke/TIA, acute limb ischaemia.
Other consequencesEmbolism (cholesterol/thrombus), aneurysm (media weakening → AAA), ischaemia of organs (renal artery stenosis, mesenteric ischaemia), peripheral arterial disease.
SitesAbdominal aorta > coronary > popliteal > internal carotid > circle of Willis.

los.text: Describe the primary surgical interventions for common cardiac conditions and post-operative care considerations
los.html:
CABG (coronary artery bypass grafting)
  • Indications: left main stem disease, multivessel disease (especially with diabetes or ↓ LV function), failed PCI.
  • Conduits: left internal mammary artery to LAD (best long-term patency ~90% at 10 years), radial artery, long saphenous vein (patency ~50–60% at 10 years).
  • On-pump (cardiopulmonary bypass) or off-pump
  • Median sternotomy.
PCI(percutaneous coronary intervention, by cardiologists, not surgery)Balloon + drug-eluting stent via radial artery → dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor, typically 6–12 months).
Valve surgery
  • Aortic valve replacement (mechanical: lifelong warfarin, durable; bioprosthetic: no long-term anticoagulation, degenerates ~10–15 years), TAVI for elderly/high-risk aortic stenosis
  • Mitral repair (preferred) or replacement
  • Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (MitraClip).
OthersAortic surgery (dissection type A, aneurysm), congenital repairs, heart transplant/LVADs, AF ablation (maze).
Post-operative care
  • ICU monitoring (arterial line, CVP, ECG)
  • Analgesia
  • Early extubation
  • Chest drains
  • Fluid/electrolyte balance (keep K⁺ >4, Mg²⁺ >1)
  • Glycaemic control
  • VTE prophylaxis
  • Early mobilisation and physio
  • Wound care (sternal precautions: no lifting/driving ~6 weeks).
ComplicationsBleeding/tamponade (↓BP, ↑CVP, muffled sounds), post-op AF (~30%), stroke, AKI, sternal wound infection/mediastinitis, pneumonia/atelectasis, delirium, post-pericardiotomy syndrome.
Long termCardiac rehabilitation, secondary prevention drugs, risk factor control.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat stable angina and acute coronary syndromes and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
sessions: Clin 4: Pharmacology of drugs in coronary disease
los.html:
Stable angina

DrugMechanismNotes
GTN (sublingual PRN) / isosorbide mononitrateNO donor → ↑ cGMP → venodilation (↓ preload) ± coronary dilationHeadache, hypotension; nitrate-free period to avoid tolerance; contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil)
β-blockers (bisoprolol, atenolol)β1 block → ↓ HR, contractility → ↓ O₂ demand, ↑ diastolic perfusion time1st line (or CCB). Avoid in asthma, heart block; fatigue, cold peripheries
CCBs: rate-limiting (verapamil, diltiazem) or dihydropyridine (amlodipine)Block L-type Ca²⁺ channels → vasodilation (± ↓ HR)Don't combine verapamil with β-blocker (heart block); use amlodipine with β-blocker
IvabradineBlocks If (funny current) in SA node → ↓ HRNeeds sinus rhythm
NicorandilK⁺ channel opener + nitrateMouth/GI/anal ulcers
Ranolazine↓ late Na⁺ currentQT
  • Secondary prevention for all: aspirin 75 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, ACEi (if diabetes, HTN, LV dysfunction), BP control, lifestyle.

ACS

AntiplateletsAspirin 300 mg loading (COX-1 irreversible → ↓ TXA2) + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor, prasugrel (PCI), clopidogrel (if bleeding risk)) → DAPT for 12 months.
AnticoagulationFondaparinux (NSTEMI unless immediate angiography) or unfractionated heparin during PCI.
Reperfusion (STEMI)
  • Primary PCI within 12 h (if achievable within 120 min of when fibrinolysis could be given)
  • Otherwise fibrinolysis (alteplase/tenecteplase; contraindications: recent bleed, stroke, surgery).
AnalgesiaIV morphine/diamorphine + antiemetic; GTN. O₂ only if sats <94%.
Post-MI("ABCDE")
  • ACEi (+/- ARB), β-blocker, Clopidogrel/ticagrelor + aspirin, Diet/lifestyle and cardiac rehab, Eplerenone (if LVEF ≤40% with HF/diabetes), plus high-intensity statin.
  • SGLT2i if HF.

los.text: Describe the main causes and pathophysiology of primary and secondary hypertension
los.html:
Primary (essential) hypertension (~90%)
  • No single cause
  • Polygenic + environment.
  • Mechanisms: ↑ salt sensitivity/renal Na⁺ retention (abnormal pressure natriuresis)
  • RAAS overactivity
  • Sympathetic overactivity
  • Endothelial dysfunction (↓ NO, ↑ endothelin)
  • Arterial stiffness (isolated systolic HTN in elderly)
  • Insulin resistance/obesity.
  • Risk factors: age, FHx, Black African/Caribbean ethnicity, obesity, high salt, alcohol, inactivity, stress.
Secondary hypertension (~10%)Suspect if young (<40), resistant (≥3 drugs), sudden onset/worsening, hypokalaemia, malignant HTN.
CategoryCausesClues
Renal (commonest)CKD, renal artery stenosis (atherosclerosis in elderly; fibromuscular dysplasia in young women), glomerulonephritis, ADPKD↑ creatinine, proteinuria; renal bruit; AKI after ACEi
EndocrinePrimary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's) (commonest endocrine cause), Cushing's, phaeochromocytoma (paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations), acromegaly, thyroid disease, hyperparathyroidismHypokalaemia + high aldosterone:renin ratio; plasma metanephrines
CardiovascularCoarctation of aortaRadio-femoral delay, arm > leg BP
DrugsNSAIDs, steroids, COCP, decongestants, ciclosporin, EPO, cocaine/amphetamines, liquorice, venlafaxine
OtherPregnancy (pre-eclampsia), OSA, alcohol
  • Diagnosis (NICE): clinic BP ≥140/90 → confirm with ABPM (≥135/85) or HBPM.
    • Stage 2 ≥150/95 (ABPM).
    • Assess target organ damage (urine ACR, fundi, ECG for LVH, U&E, HbA1c, lipids) and QRISK.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat hypertension and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
NICE NG136 algorithm
  • Step 1: ACEi or ARB if <55 and not of Black African/Caribbean origin, or any age with T2DM. CCB (amlodipine) if ≥55 or Black African/Caribbean (no diabetes).
  • Step 2: ACEi/ARB + CCB, or + thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide). (Black patients: ARB preferred over ACEi with CCB.)
  • Step 3: A + C + D.
  • Step 4 (resistant): confirm adherence and ABPM; if K⁺ ≤4.5 → spironolactone; if K⁺ >4.5 → α-blocker or β-blocker; seek specialist advice.
Targets<80 yrs: clinic <140/90 (ABPM <135/85); ≥80 yrs: <150/90. Lower targets with CKD + proteinuria, diabetes per specialist guidance.
ClassMechanismSide effects / cautions
ACEi (ramipril)↓ ACE → ↓ Ang II, ↓ aldosterone, ↑ bradykininDry cough (bradykinin), angioedema, ↑K⁺, ↑creatinine (check U&E 1–2 weeks); teratogenic; caution renal artery stenosis
ARB (losartan, candesartan)Block AT1 receptorAs ACEi but no cough
CCB (amlodipine)L-type Ca²⁺ block → arteriolar dilationAnkle oedema, flushing, headache, gum hypertrophy
Thiazide-like (indapamide)Block NCC in DCT↓Na⁺, ↓K⁺, ↑ glucose, ↑ urate (gout), ↑ Ca²⁺, impotence
SpironolactoneAldosterone antagonist↑K⁺, gynaecomastia
β-blockersβ1 block → ↓ CO, ↓ reninNot 1st line for HTN alone; fatigue, bronchospasm
α-blockers (doxazosin)α1 block → vasodilationPostural hypotension
Lifestyle for all↓ salt (<6 g/day), weight loss, exercise, ↓ alcohol, stop smoking, DASH diet.
PregnancyLabetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa (avoid ACEi/ARB).

los.text: Explain the strategies used for predicting the effects and treatment of genetic defects
los.html:
Predicting effects of genetic defects
  • Family history and pedigree (≥3 generations) → mode of inheritance → recurrence risk (e.g. AD 50%, AR 25%, X-linked: 50% of sons of carrier).
  • Genetic testing: diagnostic (affected person), predictive/presymptomatic (Huntington's, BRCA, FH), carrier testing, cascade testing of relatives, prenatal (CVS 11–14 weeks, amniocentesis from 15 weeks; NIPT cell-free fetal DNA), preimplantation genetic testing (PGT-M) with IVF, newborn screening.
  • Interpretation: penetrance and expressivity, variants of uncertain significance, genotype–phenotype correlation, polygenic risk scores.
Treatment/management strategies
  • Surveillance (colonoscopy in Lynch, MRI breast screening)
  • Risk-reducing surgery (mastectomy/salpingo-oophorectomy in BRCA)
  • Lifestyle/drug prevention (statins in FH)
  • Dietary treatment (PKU)
  • Enzyme replacement
  • Gene therapy (spinal muscular atrophy, haemophilia)
  • CFTR modulators
  • Reproductive options (PGT, donor gametes, adoption, prenatal diagnosis and termination).
Genetic counselling principlesNon-directive, informed consent, pre- and post-test counselling, psychological support.
Ethical issues
  • Autonomy and the right not to know
  • Testing children for adult-onset conditions (defer until they can consent unless there is medical benefit in childhood)
  • Confidentiality vs duty to relatives (genetic information is familial: GMC allows disclosure in some circumstances, ABC v St George's 2020)
  • Insurance and employment discrimination (UK Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance)
  • Incidental findings
  • Eugenics concerns and disability rights perspectives on prenatal testing
  • Equity of access.
